content.text: Interview prep plan
Goal: walk in knowing the company, the role, my stories, and the fundamentals cold.
Days 7-5: Research and foundations
Re-read the job description and highlight the top 5 requirements
Complete the company research brief
Update resume and tailor it to the role
Skim the fintech concepts cheat sheet
Days 4-3: Stories and technical practice
Write 6-8 STAR stories in the story bank
Work through 2-3 practice problems daily
Prepare a 90-second "tell me about yourself"
Days 2-1: Mock interviews and polish
Do at least 2 mock interviews (one behavioral, one technical)
Finalize questions to ask the interviewers
Test camera, mic, and meeting link, or plan the route
Interview day
Light review of stories, no new material
Send thank-you notes within 24 hours

Licenses held (money transmitter, bank partner, broker-dealer), compliance obligations (KYC/AML, PCI-DSS, SOC 2), and how they shape the product.

# Fintech cheat sheet

## Payments basics
- **Payment flow:** customer → merchant → payment processor/gateway → card network → issuing bank → settlement
- **Interchange:** fee paid by the merchant's bank to the card issuer on each card transaction
- **ACH:** US batch bank-to-bank transfers; cheap but slow (1-3 days)
- **Chargeback:** customer-initiated dispute that reverses a transaction
- **Idempotency:** retrying a request must not create a duplicate charge

## Compliance and risk
- **KYC:** Know Your Customer, verifying identity at onboarding
- **AML:** Anti-Money Laundering, monitoring and reporting suspicious activity
- **PCI-DSS:** security standard for handling card data
- **SOC 2:** audit of security and availability controls
- **Fraud vs. credit risk:** intent to deceive vs. inability to repay

## Business models
- Take rate, net interest margin, SaaS subscription, interchange revenue share, float income

## Metrics to know
- TPV (total payment volume), take rate, CAC, LTV, default/loss rate, approval rate, churn

## Engineering topics
- Double-entry ledgers, reconciliation, eventual consistency, audit logs, rate limiting, webhooks, retries with idempotency keys

Goal
Build awareness before the 14 November 2026 launch, turn it into trial signups and demo requests during launch week, and keep momentum for two weeks afterwards.
Audience and message

Call to action: start a free trial or book a demo
Six-week arc
Weeks 1-2 (19 Oct, 26 Oct): problem-led teasers, waitlist, podcast and demo assets
Week 3 (2 Nov): press release, demo video, early-access emails
Week 4 (9 Nov): launch on 14 Nov across all channels
Weeks 5-6 (16 Nov, 23 Nov): customer stories, webinar, retargeting and wrap-up
Success metrics
Agree the target for qualified leads

content.text: Property overview
Address, number of units, year built, mortgage lender, insurance provider and policy number. Fill these in so everything lives in one place.
Rent policy
Rent is due on the 1st of each month.
Grace period: 5 days. Late fee applies after that, per the lease.
Accepted payment methods: bank transfer, check, online portal.
Maintenance policy
Emergencies (water leak, no heat, gas smell, electrical hazard): respond same day.
Urgent repairs: respond within 48 hours.
Routine repairs: schedule within 7–10 days.
Key contacts
Insurance agent, property manager, accountant, utility providers, local code enforcement. Add numbers here.

suggestions.reason: Recurring checklist so rent, repairs and paperwork don't slip

content.text: Monthly routine
Start of month
Add this month's rows to Rent payments
Send rent reminders to tenants
Review open maintenance requests
After the grace period
Mark unpaid rent as Late and send a written notice
Apply late fees per the lease
End of month
Record repair costs and file invoices in Documents
Check leases expiring in the next 90 days
Reconcile rent received against the bank account

content.text: Move-in / move-out
Move-in

Security deposit and first month's rent received
Walk-through with dated photos of every room
Keys handed over and recorded
Tenant has emergency and maintenance contact info
Move-out
Written notice received and dated
Move-out inspection compared to move-in photos
Keys returned
Itemized deposit deductions sent within the legal deadline
Update tenant status to Former and schedule turnover cleaning

content.text: Itinerary
Tokyo (Days 1–5)
Day 1: Arrive at Haneda/Narita, get Suica cards, check in, easy dinner nearby and early night.
Day 2: Asakusa and Senso-ji, Sumida River walk, Tokyo Skytree in the evening.
Day 3: Meiji Shrine, Harajuku, Shibuya Crossing, Shibuya Sky at sunset.
Day 4: Day trip to Kamakura (Great Buddha, Enoshima) or Nikko.
Day 5: Free morning for shopping or teamLab, then pack and send luggage ahead by takkyubin.
Hakone (Day 6)
Romancecar from Shinjuku, Hakone Loop (ropeway, Lake Ashi cruise), ryokan dinner and onsen.
Kyoto (Days 7–10)
Day 7: Shinkansen to Kyoto, Gion evening stroll.
Day 8: Fushimi Inari at early morning, Kiyomizu-dera, Higashiyama streets.
Day 9: Arashiyama bamboo grove, monkey park, Kinkaku-ji.
Day 10: Day trip to Nara (deer park, Todai-ji).
Osaka (Days 11–14)
Day 11: Osaka Castle, Dotonbori street food at night.
Day 12: Universal Studios Japan or Osaka Aquarium Kaiyukan.
Day 13: Optional Himeji Castle day trip, last-minute souvenir shopping.
Day 14: Transfer to Kansai Airport (KIX) and fly home.

# Japan quick tips

- **Cash still matters**: many small restaurants, shrines and vending machines are cash-only. Carry ¥10,000–20,000 per adult.
- **IC card**: load Suica/PASMO/ICOCA into Apple/Google Wallet or buy physical cards on arrival.
- **Luggage forwarding**: send big bags between cities with *takkyubin* (about ¥2,000–3,000 each) and travel light on trains.
- **Trains**: stay quiet, no phone calls, and be at the platform early for Shinkansen. Reserve seats for 4 together.
- **Trash**: there are few public bins, so carry a small bag and take rubbish back to the hotel.
- **Shoes**: remove them in ryokan, temples with tatami and some restaurants. Wear easy slip-ons.
- **Tax-free shopping**: bring passports for tax-free purchases over ¥5,000.
- **Convenience stores** (7-Eleven, Lawson, FamilyMart) are great for quick, cheap meals and ATMs.

data.title: Project Brief: Migrating the Team Wiki to PlexiiWrite

content.text: Purpose

This brief sets out why and how we will move our existing team wiki into PlexiiWrite. It is meant to give everyone involved a shared understanding of the goals, what is and is not included, the rough sequence of work, and the main risks to manage. Details marked in brackets still need to be confirmed before the brief is circulated.
Background

Our team currently keeps its shared knowledge in [current wiki tool]. We have decided to consolidate into PlexiiWrite because [reason for the move, e.g. cost, search, integration with existing tools]. The migration is an opportunity to move content across and also to clean up what we carry forward, so that the new space starts out useful rather than cluttered.
Goals
The migration should achieve the following:
Move all content the team still relies on into PlexiiWrite with its structure, links and attachments intact.
Retire the old wiki cleanly, with a clear cutover date after which it is read-only and then archived.
Leave the new space easier to navigate than the old one, with a agreed top-level structure and a named owner for each section.
Get the whole team working in PlexiiWrite day to day, with no one still updating the old wiki after cutover.
Success will be measured by [success criteria, e.g. percentage of pages reviewed and migrated, no broken internal links, team sign-off at cutover].
Scope
In scope:
An audit of existing wiki pages to decide what to migrate, rewrite or archive.
Migration of approved pages, including formatting, images, attachments and internal links.
Setting up the PlexiiWrite structure, permissions and templates.
A short guide and a walkthrough session for the team.
Making the old wiki read-only at cutover and archiving it afterward.
Out of scope:
Rewriting content that is accurate but merely imperfect, beyond what is needed to migrate it.
Migrating other tools or document stores that sit outside the wiki, unless added later by agreement.
Integrations or automations in PlexiiWrite, which can follow as a separate piece of work.
Roles
Project owner: [name], accountable for delivery and the cutover decision.
Migration lead: [name], responsible for the audit, the move and link checks.
Section owners: [names], who review and approve the content in their area.
Team members: review their own pages when asked and adopt PlexiiWrite after cutover.
Timeline
Dates are to be confirmed once the page count and owners are known. The work runs in five phases:
Audit and structure design, by [date]. Inventory the current wiki, mark each page as migrate, rewrite or archive, and agree the new structure.
Pilot, by [date]. Move one representative section, check formatting and links, and adjust the approach.
Full migration, by [date]. Move the remaining approved content and have section owners review their areas.
Cutover, on [date]. Make the old wiki read-only, announce the change and run the team walkthrough.
Wrap-up, by [date]. Fix outstanding issues, collect feedback and archive the old wiki.
Risks and Mitigations
Content is lost or damaged in transfer. Keep the old wiki untouched until sign-off, and spot-check each migrated section against the original.
Internal links and attachments break. Include a link check in each phase and fix issues before moving on.
Section owners do not have time to review. Agree review windows up front and ask for [expected time per owner] rather than open-ended availability.
The team keeps using the old wiki after cutover. Set it to read-only on the cutover date and point it to PlexiiWrite with a clear notice.
Stale content is migrated unchecked. Use the audit to archive what is no longer needed, so the new space starts clean.
PlexiiWrite import limits or formatting differences cause rework. Test these in the pilot before committing to the full schedule.
Next Steps
Confirm the project owner, migration lead and section owners.
Fill in the bracketed items above, especially dates and success criteria.
Start the audit of the current wiki.

# Support Agent Onboarding Guide

## Welcome

Welcome to the team. This guide covers what your first week looks like, the tools you will use, and how we handle escalations. It is a working document, so if something is out of date or unclear, tell your onboarding buddy and we will fix it.

You are not expected to know everything in week one. The goal is to be comfortable with our tools, confident answering the common questions, and clear on when to hand something to someone else. Asking for help early is part of the job, not a sign you are behind.

Your onboarding buddy is [buddy name], your manager is [manager name], and the best place for quick questions is [team chat channel].

## Your first week

### Day one: getting set up

Today is about access and orientation. You will meet the team, get your accounts working, and understand what we do and who we help. Before the end of the day, confirm you can log in to every tool listed in the next section. If anything is missing, tell [IT or access contact] straight away rather than waiting.

You will also spend time with your buddy going over our product at a high level and reading a handful of recent tickets to see what good replies look like.

### Days two and three: learning by watching

You will shadow experienced agents, either live or by reviewing recorded sessions, and read through the internal knowledge base. Pay attention to how agents open a reply, how they confirm they understand the problem, and how they close a conversation. You will also start drafting replies to real tickets. A teammate will review them before anything is sent to a customer.

### Day four: handling tickets with review

You will begin answering a small queue of simple tickets, with your buddy reviewing your replies. Expect feedback on tone, accuracy and tagging. This is normal and it is the fastest way to learn.

### Day five: first independent tickets and a check-in

You will take on tickets independently, starting with the categories you have practiced most. At the end of the day you will have a short check-in with [manager name] to talk about what felt easy, what felt hard, and what to focus on in week two.

## Tools you will use

Your exact tools and logins are listed here so you have one place to look. Fill in or confirm each one with your buddy.

- The help desk or ticketing system, which is where all customer conversations live: [help desk tool]
- The internal knowledge base, for product answers and standard procedures: [knowledge base tool]
- Team chat, for questions, handoffs and urgent flags: [chat tool]
- The admin or back-office tool for looking up customer accounts: [admin tool]
- The bug or issue tracker, for logging problems for engineering: [issue tracker]
- The status page or incident channel, to check whether a known issue is already being worked on: [status page or channel]

A few habits will save you time. Search the knowledge base before writing a reply from scratch. Check the status page before investigating a problem that several customers may be reporting. Tag every ticket accurately, because those tags are how we spot patterns and decide what to fix.

## How we work tickets

Read the whole conversation before you reply, including any earlier tickets from the same customer. Restate the problem in your own words so the customer knows you understood it. Give the answer or the next step clearly, and if you cannot resolve it yourself, say what will happen next and when they will hear from us.

Our response and resolution targets are [response time target] for first replies and [resolution time target] for resolution. Your manager will explain how these are measured and how priority affects them.

On tone, write the way a helpful person speaks. Be warm, direct and specific. Avoid jargon the customer has not used themselves, and never guess at an answer. If you are not sure, say you are checking and then check.

## How we handle escalations

An escalation means handing a ticket to someone with more authority, access or expertise than you have. It is a normal part of support and nobody will think less of you for doing it. The aim is to get the customer to the right person with everything that person needs, so the customer never has to repeat themselves.

### When to escalate

Escalate when any of the following is true:

- The issue looks like a bug or outage rather than a usage question
- The customer needs something you do not have permission to do, such as a refund above your limit of [refund limit] or an account change
- The issue involves security, privacy, legal threats or a data concern
- The customer is at risk of leaving or has asked for a manager
- You have worked the ticket and still do not know the answer
- The ticket is approaching or has passed its target time and you are blocked

### Who to escalate to

| Situation | Escalate to |
|---|---|
| Suspected bug or technical fault | [engineering contact or channel] |
| Billing, refunds or payment disputes | [billing owner or team] |
| Security, privacy or legal concerns | [security or legal contact] |
| Upset customer or request for a manager | [team lead name] |
| Outage affecting multiple customers | [incident lead or channel] |

### How to escalate well

Before you hand off, write a note that someone can act on without reading the entire thread. Include:

- A one or two sentence summary of the problem
- The customer's account details or identifier
- What the customer expected and what actually happened
- Steps you have already tried and what you found
- The urgency, and why
- What you have told the customer about next steps

Then tell the customer you have passed their case to the right team, what they can expect, and roughly when. Keep the ticket assigned to you or clearly marked as waiting until the person you escalated to has confirmed they own it. After the escalation, check back on it. If there is no response within [escalation follow-up time], follow up in [chat channel] or tell [team lead name].

### Urgent situations

If something looks serious, such as a suspected data exposure, a widespread outage or a safety issue, do not wait for the normal process. Flag it immediately in [urgent channel or contact method] and then document what you know. It is always better to raise a false alarm than to sit on a real one.

## Your first 30 days

By the end of week two you should be handling most common ticket types with light review. By the end of the first month, you should be working independently, escalating confidently, and contributing to the knowledge base when you find gaps. [Manager name] will set specific goals with you at your week-one check-in and revisit them at [30-day review timing].

## Who to ask

- For day-to-day questions, ask [buddy name] or post in [team chat channel]
- For access or equipment problems, contact [IT or access contact]
- For schedule, leave or HR questions, contact [HR contact]
- For anything about performance, feedback or priorities, talk to [manager name]

If you are ever unsure whether to ask, ask.

Read the whole conversation before you reply, including any earlier tickets from the same customer. Restate the problem in your own words so the customer knows you understood it. Give the answer or the next step clearly, and if you cannot resolve it yourself, say what will happen next and when they will hear from us.

Our response and resolution targets are [response time target] for first replies and [resolution time target] for resolution. Your manager will explain how these are measured and how priority affects them.

On tone, write the way a helpful person speaks. Be warm, direct and specific. Avoid jargon the customer has not used themselves, and never guess at an answer. If you are not sure, say you are checking and then check.
How we handle escalations

An escalation means handing a ticket to someone with more authority, access or expertise than you have. It is a normal part of support and nobody will think less of you for doing it. The aim is to get the customer to the right person with everything that person needs, so the customer never has to repeat themselves.
When to escalate
Escalate when any of the following is true:
The issue looks like a bug or outage rather than a usage question
The customer needs something you do not have permission to do, such as a refund above your limit of [refund limit] or an account change
The issue involves security, privacy, legal threats or a data concern
The customer is at risk of leaving or has asked for a manager
You have worked the ticket and still do not know the answer
The ticket is approaching or has passed its target time and you are blocked
Who to escalate to

| Situation | Escalate to | |---|---| | Suspected bug or technical fault | [engineering contact or channel] | | Billing, refunds or payment disputes | [billing owner or team] | | Security, privacy or legal concerns | [security or legal contact] | | Upset customer or request for a manager | [team lead name] | | Outage affecting multiple customers | [incident lead or channel] |
How to escalate well
Before you hand off, write a note that someone can act on without reading the entire thread. Include:
A one or two sentence summary of the problem
The customer's account details or identifier
What the customer expected and what actually happened
Steps you have already tried and what you found
The urgency, and why
What you have told the customer about next steps

Then tell the customer you have passed their case to the right team, what they can expect, and roughly when. Keep the ticket assigned to you or clearly marked as waiting until the person you escalated to has confirmed they own it. After the escalation, check back on it. If there is no response within [escalation follow-up time], follow up in [chat channel] or tell [team lead name].
Urgent situations

If something looks serious, such as a suspected data exposure, a widespread outage or a safety issue, do not wait for the normal process. Flag it immediately in [urgent channel or contact method] and then document what you know. It is always better to raise a false alarm than to sit on a real one.
Your first 30 days

By the end of week two you should be handling most common ticket types with light review. By the end of the first month, you should be working independently, escalating confidently, and contributing to the knowledge base when you find gaps. [Manager name] will set specific goals with you at your week-one check-in and revisit them at [30-day review timing].
Who to ask
For day-to-day questions, ask [buddy name] or post in [team chat channel]
For access or equipment problems, contact [IT or access contact]
For schedule, leave or HR questions, contact [HR contact]
For anything about performance, feedback or priorities, talk to [manager name]
If you are ever unsure whether to ask, ask.

You design a clear, well-paced slide deck. Reply with ONLY a JSON object of the form {"title": string, "slides": [{"title": string, "bullets": string[], "notes": string, "layout": "title"|"bullets"|"section"}]}. Produce 5 to 10 slides that tell a coherent story with a beginning, middle and end. The first slide layout must be "title". Keep bullets to at most 6 short points per slide, and use an empty bullets array for title and section slides. Write one to three sentences of speaker notes per slide saying what to actually say. No markdown, no code fences, no prose outside the JSON. Write in plain, confident, human prose. Do not use em dashes or emoji. Do not use a bold label followed by a colon as a heading substitute; write real sentences. Ground every specific in what you were given. Write the prose, the structure and ordinary domain knowledge freely, because that is the draft and an empty skeleton is no use. But never present an invented specific as fact: no statistic, study finding, quotation, price, date or market figure you cannot source, and no detail about the reader's own world (their people, customers, revenue, tools, deadlines or past decisions) that the request did not supply. Where such a specific is genuinely needed and was not supplied, write a short bracketed placeholder like [launch date] or [owner name] instead of a plausible guess. A placeholder costs the user seconds to fill in; an invented figure they do not notice can reach a customer. Prefer a shorter, fully grounded draft over a fuller one that is partly fiction.

slides.notes: Welcome everyone. This session is about a small skill that saves a lot of time: writing a bug report that someone else can act on without coming back to ask questions.

slides.title: Why a good report matters
bullets: A clear report gets fixed faster
Vague reports cause back-and-forth and delay
The reader was not there when it happened
A report is a handoff, not just a complaint
Good reports help spot patterns across issues
slides.notes: Start with the reader. The person who picks this up has no context about what you saw, so everything they need has to be on the page. Every question they have to ask you is lost time for both of you.

slides.title: Start with a clear title and summary
bullets: Name the problem, not your guess at the cause
Say what happened and where in one line
Avoid titles like "Broken" or "Doesn't work"
Add a one or two sentence summary under it
Make it easy to search for later

bullets: List numbered steps from a known starting point
Include the exact input or data you used

State what actually happened

Browser, device, operating system and app version
Account or test data involved, without sharing secrets
